planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; like other earth stars this is a terrestrial bromeliad with no central tank, so water through a fast-draining, peaty potting mix rather than a cup.

directions: Cryptanthus fosterianus is one of the largest and most vigorous earth stars, native to Bahia, Brazil, forming a broad, flattened rosette of wide, wavy-margined leaves. The foliage is banded crosswise with irregular silvery-gray scurf over a coppery, reddish-brown background, giving the leaves a mottled, reptilian pattern that inspired the common name Rattlesnake Plant. Brighter indirect light intensifies the coppery banding, while lower light shifts the plant toward plainer green. This species has been used extensively as a parent in Cryptanthus hybridizing programs because of its large size and strong patterning, and it produces offsets freely at the base once mature.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus fosterianus species profile
Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — Cryptanthus culture notes

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or houseplant specimen in zone 10-12; pot in a peat- or coir-based, fast-draining mix and water the soil directly since this terrestrial species has no central cup.

directions: Cryptanthus acaulis, as its name suggests, forms a nearly stemless, flat rosette that hugs the soil surface, with narrow, finely serrated, light to medium green leaves that carry a fine coating of silvery-white scurf on the undersides. It is among the easiest and most commonly grown earth stars, tolerating a wider range of light and humidity than showier hybrids, which makes it a dependable choice for beginner terrariums and dish gardens. Small white flowers are produced in the center of the rosette but are largely inconspicuous compared to the foliage display. The species offsets readily, and pups can be separated and potted individually once they develop their own roots.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus acaulis species profile

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; unlike the flatter earth stars this cultivar grows in a more upright, vase-shaped rosette and prefers bright, indirect light to hold its variegation.

directions: Cryptanthus bromelioides 'Tricolor', commonly sold as Rainbow Star, differs from the flat, terrestrial earth stars in growing a taller, more upright and arching rosette with a habit closer to other tank bromeliads. Each strap-shaped leaf is longitudinally striped in cream-white, deep pink, and green, and new center growth often emerges in a vivid rose-pink before maturing to the full tricolor pattern. Bright, indirect light is essential to keep the pink and cream striping vivid; low light causes the variegation to fade toward plain green. It is one of the most widely grown Cryptanthus cultivars in the tropical foliage trade because of its bold, sustained color even without a flower display.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus bromelioides cultivar notes

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or dish-garden specimen in zone 10-12; this dwarf cultivar has no central tank, so water through a fast-draining, peaty mix rather than a cup.

directions: Cryptanthus 'It' is a compact, collector-favorite hybrid cultivar prized for its distinctively twisted, wavy-edged leaves, which give the small rosette a sculptural, almost ruffled appearance unlike the flatter form of most earth stars. Coloration is a soft blend of dusty pink, cream, and olive-green that intensifies with brighter indirect light. Because of its small mature size, it is especially well suited to terrariums, bottle gardens, and mixed dish plantings where larger Cryptanthus hybrids would quickly outgrow the space. Like other earth stars, it offsets at the base and is propagated by separating rooted pups after the parent rosette flowers and begins to decline.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus cultivar registry notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or terrarium specimen in zone 10-12; pot in a fast-draining, peat-based mix and water through the soil rather than a central cup.

directions: Cryptanthus 'Pink Starlite' is a widely sold variegated cultivar related to C. bivittatus, forming a compact, star-shaped rosette with each leaf marked by a broad cream-white central stripe against pink-flushed, bronze-green margins. It is one of the most commonly seen Cryptanthus cultivars in retail garden centers, often labeled simply as a starlite or earth star bromeliad, valued for its reliable color and small, manageable size. Coloration is best in bright, indirect light; deep shade causes the pink tones to fade toward plain green. Established rosettes send up offsets at the base that can be removed and potted separately once rooted.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus cultivar notes

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or dish-garden accent in zone 10-12; this terrestrial cultivar has no central tank, so water through a fast-draining, peaty potting mix.

directions: Cryptanthus 'Black Mystic' is a dark-foliaged cultivar grown for its wavy-margined leaves in deep burgundy to near-black tones, among the darkest coloration found in the genus. The near-black color is most pronounced under moderate, indirect light; stronger light can shift the leaves toward a lighter reddish-bronze, while deep shade mutes the contrast. Its flattened, star-shaped rosette habit is typical of Cryptanthus, making it a striking color accent when combined with brighter green or variegated companions in mixed terrariums and dish gardens. Offsets form readily at the base and can be divided once they have rooted.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Cryptanthus cultivar notes
Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — dark-foliage Cryptanthus cultivars
American Bromeliad Society — Cryptanthus culture guide

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; keep the central tank filled with filtered or rainwater and flush monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Vriesea 'Christiane' is a widely grown hybrid tank bromeliad developed for the florist and interior-plant trade, valued for producing a reliable flattened, sword-shaped inflorescence in warm orange-red tones above a rosette of glossy, strap-shaped green leaves. Compared to species like V. splendens, hybrids such as 'Christiane' tend to flower somewhat faster and more uniformly under greenhouse production, which has made them a mainstay of mass-market flowering bromeliad sales. The bract display persists for several weeks to a few months before fading, after which the parent rosette gradually declines and offsets emerge at the base. As with other Vriesea, keep the central cup filled with water and grow in a well-draining bark-based mix.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea hybrid cultivars

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; keep the central tank filled with filtered or rainwater and flush monthly to prevent stagnation.

directions: Vriesea 'Charlotte' is a compact hybrid tank bromeliad bred for potted flowering-plant production, forming a neat rosette of arching green leaves topped by an upright, flattened bract spike in bright orange to red. It is somewhat smaller and more compact in overall habit than species such as V. splendens or V. fosteriana, making it well suited to tabletop and windowsill display. The colorful bracts remain attractive for an extended period even as the small true flowers within them come and go. After the bloom fades the parent rosette slowly declines, and offsets that form at its base can be separated and grown on once they have their own roots.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; keep the central tank filled with filtered or rainwater and grow in a well-draining bark-based mix.

directions: Vriesea ospinae is a Colombian species notable for its erect flower spike, in which the yellow tubular flowers emerge from bracts strikingly marked with alternating bands of red-orange and near-black, a pattern distinct from the solid-colored or mottled bracts of most other cultivated Vriesea. The foliage forms a broad, spreading rosette of glossy mid-green leaves typical of tank-forming bromeliads. Because it originates from mid-elevation cloud forest, it appreciates slightly cooler nights and consistently high humidity compared to lowland Vriesea species. The striped inflorescence remains showy for an extended period, and mature plants produce offsets at the base once flowering finishes.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea ospinae species profile
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Colombian bromeliad collection notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or small terrarium specimen in zone 10-12; keep the small central tank filled with filtered or rainwater and grow in a well-draining bark-based mix.

directions: Vriesea racinae is a diminutive Brazilian species that stays small enough to grow comfortably in a modest pot, forming a compact rosette of soft green, slightly recurved leaves. A slender, upright flower spike bearing yellow-orange tubular flowers rises well above the foliage relative to the plant's small size, giving a disproportionately showy display for such a compact species. Because of its small mature footprint, it suits growers with limited windowsill or shelf space who still want a true tank-forming Vriesea rather than one of the larger species. Like its relatives, it is grown in a fast-draining epiphytic mix with the central cup kept topped up with water.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea racinae species profile
Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies — dwarf Vriesea species notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; keep the central tank filled with filtered or rainwater and grow in a well-draining bark-based mix.

directions: Vriesea scalaris differs from most cultivated Vriesea in its inflorescence, which is not a single flattened sword but a branching, zigzag spray of slender flower stalks bearing bright yellow blooms, a form that gives the species its name ('scalaris' meaning ladder-like). The foliage rosette is made up of thin, glossy, light green, gently arching leaves that are more delicate in texture than the broader, banded leaves of species such as V. splendens or V. fenestralis. The airy, branched flower spray held on slender, reddish-tinged stems creates a lighter, more graceful display than the bold sword-shaped bracts typical of the genus. It is grown under the same general conditions as other tank-forming Vriesea, with the central cup kept filled and the roots in a fast-draining, well-aerated mix.
sources: Bromeliad Society International — Vriesea scalaris species profile
